The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. The Pellows, who farmed the place before her father, had built it with a through-stone every yard, and her tractor had passed it for thirty years without a scrape. What caused the collapse was frost. A hard January had lifted the stones at its base, and Maren's ram stood in the gap as if he owned it.

Dell Haskett drove up from the fencing yard in Orley with wire in his truck and the cost written on a card. He said his fence posts went in below any frost and would hold a ram. Maren heard him out, then walked him down to the stream, where a row of old posts stood black and soft at the water's edge. On the way back she made her choice. She called the price of his fence fair, said she had all the help she needed, and pointed at me. That was how I came to join the work.

At first I thought the job was mostly lifting. Maren taught me to lay each stone with its length running into the wall, to pack the hearting tight, and to lean both faces in toward each other. When my fingers went numb she sent me to brush pitch onto the new gatepost, and I learned that a black, sticky job can also be the warm one.

By March the gap was one capstone short. Maren set the last one, stepped back, and balanced her wool hat on top of it. "Now it is the best-dressed wall in the parish," she said. She made me shake hands with it, and the two of us stood in the sleet laughing until the ram wandered up to look.

Maren called it the hardest winter in ten years, and I spent most of it kneeling in mud. What I took away was the ability to read a wall. When I pass one now I look for the through-stones and the lean of the faces, and I can tell within a yard where the frost will find it next.

In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Half the posts had rotted to stumps, and the commissioners wanted to know whether Rudd's line was still true.

Measuring from the tower of Sallow church, Varne found Rudd's posts standing in dry pasture a quarter of a mile above the nearest reeds, with sheep grazing around them. Year by year the river's silt had built the marsh outward. He drove his own cedar stakes along the line of dried reeds, while his chainman, Jonah Pell, followed in the punt.

Varne carried a first draft of the map, and at every stake he waited until a farmer and a reed-cutter had read it side by side. Through July both sides walked the line with him, arguing loudest where the creek bent, and by August every stake had been seen by a man from each.

The line ended at Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel. When Pell asked whose initials he should cut on the stake there, Varne handed him the knife. "Cut yours above mine, Jonah, because you carried the chain over every rod of this marsh."

That autumn the highest tides rose to the cedar stakes and stopped, as the reeds had said they would. In November farmers and reed-cutters signed the map together, and the quarrel that had outlasted Rudd ended with it. The commissioners hung the map in the Wexcombe courthouse, where Varne's line can still be read.

passage:
When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, promptly wrote the address of the county archive across the lid in black marker.

Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street and keeps its piano as it was in the early years, telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere, who came the next week. The archivist found the reel sound and supple, though film that old, she said, can catch fire near a hot lamp. When she asked for an empty spool, Brask sent one across the lobby with a gentle underhand pitch. Colm, holding a frame to the window, was the first to recognize the street and place it in town: their grandfather’s hardware sign hung over a doorway.

The archive’s laboratory had a waiting list, and the delay stretched through the summer while a collector in the city wrote twice offering to buy it. The archive paid for the copy out of its own money, so Brask had only the waiting to bear.

Brask wanted live music, and the only person in Carrow who had ever played for silent films was Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist. She had not set foot in the building in forty years. Ines and Colm argued with Brask that a recording would do, but he called at Mabel’s house three evenings running, and on the fourth she came down and asked him to run the copy for her privately while she found the music.

In October the copy was screened at the Lantern to a full house, and the reel showed the town exactly what the pencilled lid had promised. The original stayed in Dunmere, where everyone agreed it belonged. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She told him she would, as long as the original reel stayed locked in the archive’s vault and was never carried into the Lantern’s hot little booth.
